summary: Defines a Network Debugging Protocol to be used in an implementation of a PDP-11 network bootstrap device and a cross-network debugger.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets a programmer on one computer fix and start a small faraway computer over the network.

subtitle: Remote debugging protocol for PDP-11 systems over the network

tldr.problem: Software developers need to debug and control PDP-11 processes running on distant computers without direct access to the machine.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Debugging Protocol defines a message format and command set that a remote host uses to instruct a PDP-11 to perform debugging operations: depositing memory, examining registers, setting breakpoints, resuming execution, and reporting process state changes.
tldr.outcome: The protocol enables cross-network debugging, allowing a developer at one site to control execution of a process at another, including breakpoint management and memory examination.

today: RFC 643 describes a pioneering approach to remote debugging that preceded modern debuggers. While the specific protocol is historical, the concept of remote process control and the state vector representation remain relevant to modern debugging tools.

sections.title: Remote Debugging Over the Network
sections.content:
RFC 643 defines a protocol for debugging PDP-11 processes running on remote hosts via network commands. The protocol is designed for use with PDP-11 systems running an operating system capable of performing low-level debugging tasks like setting and removing breakpoints and single-stepping instructions. A subset can be used on standalone programs with fewer debugging capabilities.

The protocol operates as a level-2 protocol, bypassing the standard HOST-HOST protocol. Messages are exchanged on a single link (377 octal) between a remote debugger and the PDP-11. Commands from the remote host request actions like stopping a process or examining memory, and responses confirm success or indicate that a process has trapped or hit a breakpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: A programmer sends commands over the network to a distant computer telling it to pause, check memory, or start running again. The distant computer sends back what it finds.

sections.title: Command Structure
sections.content:
Each command consists of an 8-bit operation code, an 8-bit process identifier, two 16-bit arguments, and an optional byte string. The operation code from the PDP-11 response mirrors the command code for successful completion, or has the 200 bit set to indicate failure (CAN'T reply). An operation code with the 100 bit set indicates an asynchronous event—a process has stopped for a reason other than a command from the remote host.

Commands include NOP (no operation), DEBUG (begin debugging a process), STOP (halt a running process), DEPOSIT (write bytes to memory), EXAMINE (read bytes from memory), BREAK (set a breakpoint), UNBREAK (remove a breakpoint), and SINGLE STEP. Asynchronous replies include TRAP (process terminated abnormally), HALT (process terminated normally), BPT (hit breakpoint), and TTRAP (trace trap from single step).
sections.plainLanguage: Commands are short messages with an operation number, process number, and data. Replies say whether the command worked or what happened to the process.

sections.title: Debugging Workflow
sections.content:
A debugging session begins with a DEBUG command to claim control of a process; the PDP-11 responds DEBUGGING if successful or CAN'T DEBUG if another remote host is already debugging it. Once debugging, the remote host can issue commands to examine memory (EXAMINE), modify memory (DEPOSIT), set breakpoints (BREAK), or single-step execution (SINGLE STEP). When a breakpoint is hit or a process traps, the PDP-11 sends an asynchronous reply with the complete state vector for the process—the values of all registers and program counter. Process creation and destruction are also supported, allowing the remote host to create a fresh process for debugging.

The protocol assumes the PDP-11 can manage its own breakpoint tables, remember which remote host is debugging each process, and report process state changes. The remote host is responsible for maintaining the state of the debugging session and issuing appropriate follow-up commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The programmer asks to debug a program, then sends commands to pause it, check values, set traps, or step through code one line at a time. The computer reports back what it finds.
